content.title: Lifelong learning, long-lasting impact
content.summary: For the last 16 years Muneerah Vastani, currently Assistant Professor at the School of Nursing and Midwifery in East Africa, has been guiding young nurses in their research and clinical interests.

content.text: For the last 16 years Muneerah Vastani, currently Assistant Professor at the School of Nursing and Midwifery in East Africa, has been guiding young nurses as they learn to nurture their patients back to health and conduct research into the science of early childhood development.
This investigation into the first few years of a child's life, which has a substantial impact on the future adult, helps Muneerah view nursing in a broader, more holistic sense.
To her nursing is a "tool" to prevent illness in the young, to combat the developmental delays associated with poverty and to raise awareness about important health issues in society.

Muneerah is now eager to strengthen the impact of her research by pursuing a PHd at the University of Alberta, Canada, on the roles and responsibilities of nurses in supporting early childhood development.

Most nurses in Tanzania and East Africa do not have the chance for further studies and Muneerah is keen to use this opportunity to identify novel ways to make a difference. She believes a PhD will help her make a much more significant contribution to the region.

Commenting on her long-term plans, she said: "Several nurses have retired with a diploma. Few have gone up to degree level and very few have attained a master's degree... My plan is to return to Africa - preferably East Africa - with more capacity and vigor to prevent diseases and fight poverty."

"When I come back, I want to advocate for early childhood development. This is one area that governments need to put more money in, if they are to deal with poverty. When you have a healthy child, you have a healthy nation."
Muneerah's longstanding association with the AKU has exposed her to the clinical service, research and community healthcare possibilities that nursing can provide.

Earlier this year, the University made a major investment to raise standards in nursing teaching and practice in East Africa when it opened the new home of its School of Nursing and Midwifery at Salama House in Dar es Salaam. To date, more than 2,100 nurses in East Africa have graduated from the AKU and moved on to improving healthcare in the real world.
